sentences.text: Spiclypeus was a large ceratopsian estimated to be 4.5 to 6 meters long and to weigh about three to four tonnes.
The reconstructed skull of this animal measures 167 centimeters in length.
A triangular horn on the nose of the skull is 166 millimeters long.
The brow horns measure 228 millimeters on the left side and 246 millimeters on the right.
This species is unique among chasmosaurines for having a wrinkled surface where the rear projection of the premaxilla makes contact.
It also possesses a specific set of traits, including sideways-projecting brow horns, fused epiparietals at the base, and distinct curling patterns on the front frill horns.
Parallel injuries on the frill suggest that an opponent's brow horns once pierced the shield bone during a fight.
A severe infection affected the entire lower half of the left humerus, causing dysfunction in the joint surface due to a large abscess.
The body reacted to this humerus infection by remodeling the bone and rotating the joint over 90 degrees from its normal orientation.
The Spiclypeus specimen was discovered in September 2005 by Bill D. Shipp on his ranch in Montana.
The land where the fossil was found was purchased in 2000 by Bill D. Shipp, a nuclear physicist.
The excavation team secured all remaining bones of the specimen by 2007.
Amateur paleontologist Joe Small was hired to excavate the Spiclypeus fossils after they were found.
The genus Spiclypeus was named by Mallon et al. in 2016.
Analysis of growth lines in the femur indicates a minimum age of ten years for the holotype specimen.
The type specimen of Spiclypeus shows a significant infection on its frill, hypothesized by some to be an injury inflicted by a rival of the same species.
Perforations in the frill of the Spiclypeus holotype are likely the result of intraspecific combat where an opponent's brow horns pierced the bone.
Extensive bone remodeling suggests the infection was not immediately lethal and may have been caused by a less virulent form of tuberculosis or fungus.
Spiclypeus belongs to the family Ceratopsidae.
The parent group of Spiclypeus is the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
Spiclypeus was classified in the subfamily Chasmosaurinae in 2016.
Spiclypeus is the sister species to a clade containing Kosmoceratops and Vagaceratops, rather than being closely related to Triceratops.
Phylogenetic analysis places Spiclypeus as a sister species to a clade containing Kosmoceratops and Vagaceratops, rather than in the Triceratops branch.
Spiclypeus lived between 76.24 and 75.21 million years ago in the lower Coal Ridge Member of the Judith River Formation.
Spiclypeus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 76 million years ago in the Campanian stage.
Spiclypeus lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether Spiclypeus, Ceratops montanus, and Pentaceratops aquilonius might represent a single species, though this cannot be confirmed due to fragmentary fossils.
